For any two vertices, their discovery/finish intervals are either entirely disjoint or one nests completely inside the other — never partially overlapping. A vertex is a proper descendant of another exactly when its interval nests inside it.
An edge from a vertex to one of its own ancestors in the DFS tree — is that a tree edge, a back edge, a forward edge, or a cross edge?

Tree edges are part of the DFS tree itself. Back edges point to an ancestor, closing a cycle. Forward edges point to an already-finished descendant. Cross edges point to neither — a different subtree, or a different DFS tree entirely. All four are defined purely from discovery and finish times and tree membership, nothing else.

syllabus.clause: three-colour cycle detection in directed graphs and parent-check in undirected graphs

at.step: A directed graph has a cycle exactly when its DFS finds a back edge — an edge to a vertex still grey, still on the current path. An undirected graph needs no colouring at all: a visited neighbour that is not the immediate parent is already a cycle, because an undirected DFS never has the cross edges that could confuse the test.

syllabus.clause: iterative DFS with an explicit stack to avoid recursion-depth limits

at.step: A recursive DFS on a long dependency chain — a few hundred thousand vertices deep — overflows the call stack before the algorithm's own logic is ever wrong. Converting to an explicit stack of (vertex, iterator) pairs, instead of the language's own call stack, gives the identical traversal order and finishes without crashing.

items.item: DFS and BFS both run in O(n+m) and visit every vertex exactly once; the topic's own contrast with Chapter 17's first topic is purely about order (deep-first vs. level-by-level), never about asymptotic cost

at.step: A breadth-first frontier answers one question well: the fewest edges to reach a vertex. It says nothing about which vertex to visit next when the graph has structure a single widening ring can't see. Depth-first search goes the other way entirely: as deep as possible before ever backing up.

items.item: A DFS finish order, reversed, gives a valid topological order on a DAG for free — no back edges means no cycle, and the reversal is the only extra step needed, which is exactly topic 61's own reverse-DFS-finish-order algorithm

at.step: A directed graph with no back edges — no cycle anywhere — has a DFS finish order that is itself a valid answer to a question BFS was never asked: in what order can every vertex be processed so that nothing is processed before the things it depends on. That order falls out of the traversal just built, almost for free.

items.item: The explicit-stack conversion generalises beyond DFS to any recursive tree or graph algorithm whose call depth can exceed a language's recursion limit, making it a reusable technique, not a one-off DFS trick
